item.title: Filling an OpenDocument Template
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: How officeParser 8.7.0 fills .odt and .ott templates with the same tags and data as Word's: tags split across spans, spaces stored as elements, blocks over list items and heading rows, and fresh names for every copy a loop makes.
item.content:encoded:
officeParser 8.7.0 fills OpenDocument text templates, .odt and .ott, with the same tags and data as Word templates, through the same OfficeTemplate.render, tags() and check().

The tag language was never the hard part. The engine that pairs blocks and walks the data does not care which format it is in, so I moved everything Word-specific out of it into a dialect, and wrote OpenDocument's. This post is about what that dialect had to know: where an ODT keeps its text, how a tag gets split, why a 22-byte element is read as 16 spaces, and why every copy a loop makes needs new names.

A Small Template

I built a template by hand, as an .ott: a greeting whose tag LibreOffice would have split across a span, a reference after a long run of spaces, a loop over list items, a loop over table rows below a heading row, and a loop over a paragraph holding a bookmark, a footnote and a comment. The header holds {{ company }} statement. Then: 

const data = {
    company: 'Acme',
    name: 'Ada',
    ref: 'INV-7',
    tasks: ['Sign', 'Return'],
    lines: [{ item: 'Bolts', qty: 2 }, { item: 'Nuts', qty: 5 }],
    people: [{ name: 'Ann' }, { name: 'Bob' }, { name: 'Cy' }],
};
const out = await OfficeTemplate.render(templatePath, { data });

Read back with parseOffice and written as text, the long run of spaces shortened to its count:

Dear Ada,
Reference[256 spaces]INV-7
To do: Sign
To do: Return

| Item  | Qty | 
| Bolts | 2   | 
| Nuts  | 5   | 

Ann
Bob
Cy
Checked.


--- Notes ---
About Ann
About Bob
About Cy

I then opened the result in LibreOffice 7.3, headless, and printed it to PDF. It opened, the header read "Acme statement", and LibreOffice numbered the three copied footnotes 1, 2 and 3.

What an ODT Keeps Where

An ODT is a zip, like a DOCX, but flatter. There are no relationship files: parts are found by name.

PartWhat it holdsWhat a render does to it
mimetypeThe package's media type, as plain textWrites it first and stored, not compressed; switches a template's type to a document's
META-INF/manifest.xmlEvery part and its media type, the package's own under the path /Switches the root's media type for an .ott; drops encryption data for a template that was decrypted
content.xmlThe body, with the notes, comments and text boxes inside the paragraphs that hold themFills tags
styles.xmlStyles, and the master pages, which hold the headers and footersFills tags
meta.xml, pictures, the restTitle, author and the like; mediaCopied as they are

Word keeps each header in a part of its own (word/header1.xml); OpenDocument keeps them all with the page styles, so tags() gives the sample's header tag, {{ company }}, the part styles.xml. The mimetype entry must come first and stored, so the type can be read at a fixed place near the start of the file without unzipping. The sample's entries come out as mimetype, META-INF/manifest.xml, content.xml, styles.xml, mimetype at compression method 0.

A Tag Split Across Spans

In what is actually inside a DOCX I described Word's runs: text sits in a <w:t> inside a <w:r>, and a new run starts at every change of formatting, so a typed {{name}} can arrive in three. OpenDocument splits the same way with less markup. Text sits straight in the paragraph, and only a stretch with formatting of its own is wrapped, in a <text:span>. Type {{name}}, make two letters italic, and the paragraph is: 

<text:p>Dear {{<text:span text:style-name="T1">na</text:span>me}},</text:p>

The engine reads a paragraph as a list of runs. In a DOCX a run is the text of one <w:t>; in an ODT it is each stretch of character data directly inside a paragraph (text:p, text:h) or inside a span, a link (text:a) or a text:meta in it. The runs of one paragraph are joined, the tags are found in the joined text, and each run a tag touched gets a marker: the first stands for the tag, the others for nothing. So the value goes where the tag began, and takes that place's formatting. Here the tag began outside the span, so Ada is not italic, and the span is left behind, empty: 

<text:p>Dear Ada<text:span text:style-name="T1"></text:span>,</text:p>

A note, a comment or a text box sits inside the paragraph that holds it, but its paragraphs are its own: a tag never runs from the paragraph into its footnote. Some text is never read for tags at all: the text of a field such as text:date, a note's citation, a comment's author and date, and deleted text kept for tracked changes.

Spaces That Are Elements

OpenDocument folds white space as HTML does: two spaces in a row read as one. A second space is kept as an element, <text:s/>, and a run of them as one element with a count, <text:s text:c="5"/>. A tag typed with spaces carries them in that form, and may be split across a span besides: 

template: <text:p>Hello {{<text:s/>who<text:span text:style-name="T1"><text:s text:c="2"/></text:span>}}!</text:p>
rendered: <text:p>Hello Ann<text:span text:style-name="T1"></text:span>!</text:p>

A value is written back the same way, so it reads as typed. Here is one with a tab, three spaces and a new line, in [{{ v }}]: 

value:    'Qty:\t2   pcs\nboxed'
rendered: [Qty:<text:tab/>2 <text:s text:c="2"/>pcs<text:line-break/>boxed]

The count is where my first version went wrong, on the 8.7.0 branch before the release, so no published version did this. It read <text:s text:c="256"/> as the 256 spaces it stands for. That element is 22 bytes. Every limit on a template is a limit on its XML: the parts' sizes, the number of elements. A paragraph's text had never been longer than its XML, so those limits also bounded the text, and with it every pass the engine makes over the text. A run of spaces broke that: 22 bytes became 256 characters, 11.6 times, and a large part of such runs could pass the longest string V8 will make.

So the engine now reads a long run short and writes it back whole. A <text:s/> is read as at most 16 spaces, and the run keeps the count it stood for. <text:s/> is 9 characters and reads as 1; any element with a count is at least 20 characters. The text is never longer than its XML again, and a tag needs no more: the only spaces it looks at are its own and its delimiters'. Where the caller's delimiters hold more than 7 spaces in a row, the limit rises to twice that run plus one, so a run read short still holds the end of one tag and the start of the next. The spaces not read are written back where no tag is: in the run's text outside tags, or between the tag ending in it and the tag starting in it. Here is a run of 999,999 spaces, 25 bytes of XML, between two tags: 

template: <text:p>{{ a }}<text:s text:c="999999"/>{{ b }}</text:p>
rendered: <text:p>left<text:s text:c="999999"/>right</text:p> (1 ms)

The element goes out as it came in, 25 bytes standing for the same million spaces. (The time is the whole render, as the script measured it on my M1 Pro under Node 24.)

What a Block Can Cover

Where a block's tags sit decides what it covers, as in Word: both tags in one paragraph, the text between them; in paragraphs side by side, the paragraphs between them, a paragraph holding nothing but a tag removed with it; in different cells of one table, whole rows. OpenDocument adds two places.

  • List items. Tags in items of one list cover the items between them, and an item holding nothing but a tag goes with it. In the sample, three items ({{ for t in tasks }}, To do: {{ t }}, {{ endfor }}) became two: "To do: Sign" and "To do: Return".
  • Heading rows. A table's heading rows, the ones repeated on every page, sit in a table:table-header-rows of their own. A loop inside them repeats there: one over Q1 and Q2 left two heading rows. A block that starts in the heading rows and ends in the body is refused, rather than writing a table whose heading rows are torn open: 
TEMPLATE_SYNTAX: [OfficeParser]: Template tag '{{ for h in heads }}' in content.xml and the other tags of its block do not
enclose content together: one is in a table's heading rows and another is not.

Afterwards the part is repaired where loops and branches left it invalid: a table or group of rows with no row is removed, and a cell, header, footer, note, text box or comment with no paragraph gets an empty one (a style:header left empty would also hide the left-page header in LibreOffice). A bookmark whose end went with a branch is closed after its start.

Copies Need Fresh Names

A loop copies content, and content carries names that must be unique: an xml:id any element may have, a note's text:id, the names of bookmarks, reference marks, comments, frames, tables and sections, a drawing's draw:id. Each first write keeps its name. Each later copy gets the name with a number, person_2, counted past every name the template already holds, and a range's end follows its start.

To see what is at stake, I wrote the sample's loop paragraph three times by hand with its names unchanged, as a copy that ignored them would, and let LibreOffice 7.3 open and save it. Then I did the same with the render's output:

In each copyNames kept, after LibreOfficeRendered, after LibreOffice
Paragraph xml:idperson; the other two droppedperson, person_2, person_6
Bookmarkwho, who1, who2, renamed by LibreOfficewho, who_3, who_7
FootnoteAll threeAll three
Comment, its range ending after the loop"Check Ann" only"Check Ann", "Check Bob", "Check Cy"

Nothing was refused. LibreOffice opened every file and dropped or renamed what clashed, silently. The notes survived either way. The comments are worth a closer look. A comment can cover a range: office:annotation where it starts, holding its text, and office:annotation-end with the same name where it ends. In the sample the comment starts inside the loop and ends after it, in "Checked.". Written three times under one name, with one end, LibreOffice kept the first comment and lost the other two and their text. (Without the end, it kept all three.)

A range across a loop's edge has one start and one end, so the render writes it once. Most of what a range is made of is then left out of the later copies. A comment cannot, since it holds its text, so each later copy is written as a comment of its own, on a point, under a fresh name: 

<office:annotation office:name="c1">...Check Ann...</office:annotation>
<office:annotation office:name="c1_5">...Check Bob...</office:annotation>
<office:annotation office:name="c1_9">...Check Cy...</office:annotation>
<text:p>Checked.<office:annotation-end office:name="c1"/></text:p>

One more place needed a name. A block may cut through a span, a link or a text:meta: the element is closed before the cut and opened again after it. The half after the cut is a second element, so when the element has an xml:id, that half gets one of its own.

A Template Becomes a Document

An .ott is an .odt with another media type: application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text-template in mimetype and on the manifest's root entry. Filling one gives a document, not another template, so the render switches both to application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text, as the sample's output shows. Nothing else in the manifest, or in meta.xml, changes. A password-protected template is decrypted with password or onPassword, and the document is written plain, its manifest without the encryption data.

What It Does Not Do Yet

  • Presentations and spreadsheets are not templates yet. A .pptx, .odp, .xlsx or .ods passed to OfficeTemplate.render rejects with TEMPLATE_UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT. Of the two, slides are the easier; in spreadsheets, moving the rows below a loop, with the formulas, merged cells and print areas that point at them, is the real work.
  • A <text:tab/> or <text:line-break/> typed inside a tag is read as nothing, and a quoted string in a tag holding more than 16 spaces in a row reads as 16, the bound on <text:s/>.

item.title: Text That Looks Like a Tag: When Data for People Meets a Template for Machines
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: How officeParser 8.7.0 reports template text that only looks like a tag without flagging braces in prose, code or JSON, and how it reads numbers with a decimal comma, numbers stored as text and block keywords spelt as other template languages spell them.
item.content:encoded:
A Word template says "Dear {{first name}},". The data has a first name column, because the data came from a spreadsheet and that is what the column is called. Render it with officeParser 8.6.0 and every letter says "Dear {{first name}}," with nothing filled in and nothing said. The tag was never a tag: a field's name has no spaces, so the engine read it as prose between braces, and prose is written as typed.

This post is about what 8.7.0 does with text that only looks like a tag, how it tells that apart from braces that are just prose, code or JSON, and the other places where data written for people meets a template written for machines: numbers with a decimal comma, numbers stored as text, and block keywords spelt the way another template language spells them.

Four Ways to Almost Write a Tag

Here is a template with four near misses and one real tag, made from Markdown with officeParser's own converter, then listed with OfficeTemplate.tags() and rendered: 

Dear {{first name}},
Your order {{ order } ships on {{ date }}.
Total: {{ total | fromat "0.00" }}
Nom : ｛｛nom｝｝

What tags() lists, kind, tag and reason:

text "{{first name}}" space-in-name
text "{{ order }" missing-delimiter
field "{{ date }}"
text "{{ total | fromat \"0.00\" }}" unknown-filter
text "｛｛nom｝｝" full-width

And what render() gives with data holding every one of those values, a first name, an order, a total and a nom: 

warning: TEMPLATE_NOT_A_TAG {"texts":[{"text":"{{first name}}","part":"word/document.xml","reason":"space-in-name"}, ... ],"found":4}
Dear {{first name}},
Your order {{ order } ships on 9 November.
Total: {{ total | fromat "0.00" }}
Nom : ｛｛nom｝｝

The document is what 8.6.0 would write. What changed is that it is no longer silent. tags() lists each near miss as kind: 'text' with a reason, and render() and check() raise one TEMPLATE_NOT_A_TAG warning per call with each text, its part and its reason. The four reasons are exactly these:

ReasonExampleWhat it is
space-in-name{{first name}}A name with white space in it: letters, digits, _ . - and spaces, starting with a letter or _, at most 64 characters
unknown-filter{{ total | fromat "0.00" }}A field through a word after | that is no filter, built in or in formatters
missing-delimiter{{ name }, { name }}A name between delimiters one of which is a character short
full-width｛｛nom｝｝Delimiters typed with full-width characters, as a Japanese or Chinese keyboard types them

It is a warning, not an error, because 8.6.0 rendered every one of these templates and some such text is meant. Refusing them would break templates that work.

Braces That Are Just Braces

The first two reasons are easy, because they sit between whole delimiters, where the engine already looks for tags. The hard one is missing-delimiter. A template can hold code, JSON, set notation and sentences with braces in them, and none of that may be reported. Each line below is a template of its own, with what tags() lists as text: 

Use {x} or { x } in a set.                      -> nothing
Send `{"name": {"first": "Ana"}}` as the body.  -> nothing
const o = {a: {b}};                             -> nothing
A pair of sets: {{x}, {y}}.                     -> nothing
An empty {{}} stays.                            -> nothing
Dear {{ name }, welcome.                        -> {{ name } (missing-delimiter)
Dear { name }}, welcome.                        -> { name }} (missing-delimiter)
Dear {{ name }, see {x}.                        -> {{ name } (missing-delimiter)
Dear {{ name }, see {x}}.                       -> nothing

Look at {{x}, {y}}. Read alone, {{x} is a start delimiter, a name and an end one character short, and {y}} is the same the other way round. Together they are a set of two sets. The difference is balance: the brace {{x} leaves open, a later one closes.

So officeParser counts braces, typed as stored, as a stack. The start's character opens one. The end's character closes one when any is open, so the count never goes below zero. A near miss opens its own start characters and then closes its own end characters, the same way. Then:

  • A short start ({ name }}) is not reported inside braces still open, or right after the start's own character.
  • A short end ({{ name }) that leaves some of its braces open is pending: it is code if a later brace closes everything it left open, and reported if anything is still open at the end of the paragraph. That is why the last two lines above differ by one brace.
  • A short end that leaves nothing open is reported at once. Nothing later can make it balance.

This is only done for delimiters of one character typed twice or more each side, such as the default {{ and }}, where "one character short" means something. With delimiters of one character for both ends, such as $$ and $$, a character both opens and closes, so it balances nothing, and braces are not counted: 

Total $5. Dear $ name $$   [$$ $$]   -> $ name $$ (missing-delimiter)

One Pass, and the Version That Was Wrong

A template is input a caller may not control, so the scan has to be linear. It walks the paragraph's text once and stops only at a character a delimiter can start with, its full-width form, or, when braces are counted, a closing brace. Each stop looks ahead at most a delimiter, a name of up to 64 characters and another delimiter, and builds nothing but that short name. Pending short ends sit on a stack whose levels rise strictly, so each is pushed once and popped once. I timed the scan alone, one run each on my M1 Pro under Node 24, on three of the shapes the tests use, at two lengths:

ParagraphSmallerTwice the length
{{a} repeated, every one left open2.0M characters, 43 ms4.0M characters, 66 ms
{{a} repeated, then as many }1.3M characters, 27 ms2.5M characters, 53 ms
{{ a }}} repeated, end delimiter }}}}2.0M characters, 25 ms4.0M characters, 48 ms

It did not start out like this. 8.7.0 went through rounds of review before release, and the scan was rewritten twice. The first version visited every character and allocated at each, five times the cost of reading the text. It charged each near miss against the template's XML element limit, so plain text that 8.6.0 rendered was refused. And it reported both halves of {{x}, {y}}. The fix counted braces.

That counting is what the fourth round found broken. It applied each near miss to the depth as one signed number, the start characters it opens minus the end characters it closes, and it made every short end pending. That holds while the end is no longer than the start. With {{ and }}}, {{ name }} is a short end that opens two and closes two: it leaves nothing open, but it was still made pending at the depth it found, and the next unrelated closing brace closed it as code. Dear {{ name }}, see {x}. reported nothing; 8.7.0 as released reports {{ name }} there. With }}}}, the net was negative and the depth went below zero. Past the 1,000 near misses a template lists, pending ends were kept in a bit set, a bit per depth, and a depth of -1 became word -1 >>> 5, 134,217,727: an array of 512 MB for one paragraph. Listed and unlisted pending ends also followed different rules, so the same text was counted only once the list was full.

That was two representations of one idea, and a signed number only one branch kept above zero. The fix replaced them with one stack and wrote down what must stay true:

  • The depth never falls below zero and never exceeds the start characters read.
  • Only a short end that leaves its own braces open is pending, at the depth before it.
  • Pending levels rise strictly, so when one is closed, every one above it is closed too.
  • Each pending entry is pushed once and closed or reported once, so the count is exact.

The scan is now tested against a reference written as plainly as possible: braces are objects on an explicit stack, each near miss owns the braces it opens, and a pending one is reported if one of its braces is still on the stack at the end. It is quadratic, which is fine for short random texts. The suite runs 20,000 texts in its fast mode and 200,000 in full, each with room for 0, 1, 2, 3 and 1,000 listings. Here, 20,000 texts, 10,645 of them with near misses, gave no differences in 564 ms on the same machine.

A Thousand, Then a Count

Each listing takes a few hundred bytes for a few characters of text, so a template lists at most 1,000 and counts the rest. A template of 1,500 paragraphs, Row 0: {{ value 0 }} to Row 1499: {{ value 1499 }}: 

tags() listed 1000 texts
warning: TEMPLATE_NOT_A_TAG found 1500 listed 1000
  1500 texts that look like template tags are not tags and are written as typed (only the first 1000 are listed): ...

tags() lists, and raises the warning only when its list was cut. The 1,000 are for the whole template. Notes that only loops refer to are compiled on their own, and earlier on the 8.7.0 branch they took a second room of 1,000; one room now serves every part.

Numbers Written for People

Data from a German or Brazilian spreadsheet writes one thousand two hundred and thirty-four and a half as 1.234,50, and French data as 1 234,50. In 8.6.0 that was text, not a number, and a number picture refused it. 8.7.0 reads it with dataNumberSeparators. The template here is Total: {{ total | format "#,##0.00" }}:

DataConfigResult
"1.234,50"noneTEMPLATE_DATA_INVALID (unformattable)
"1.234,50"dataNumberSeparators: { decimal: ',', group: '.' }Total: 1,234.50
"12,50"the sameTotal: 12.50
"1.5", "1.50"the sameunformattable
"0.500"the sameunformattable
"1234.567"the sameunformattable
"1 234,50" (no-break space){ decimal: ',', group: ' ' }Total: 1,234.50

The refusals are the point. With . for groups, 1.5 could be one and a half written the English way, or a typo. Rather than guess, a group separator must be followed by groups of exactly three digits, and the first group is one to three digits. The first group also may not start with 0. That rule came from review before the release: until then, 0.001 was read as 1 and 0.500 as 500, text written with a decimal point read as a grouped integer. A grouped integer never starts with 0, so 0.500 is now refused.

The rule cannot catch everything. With the same setting, "1.500" is fifteen hundred, as German data means it. If the data mixes both ways of writing numbers, no setting can read it right.

numberSeparators, which existed before, says how a picture writes numbers. It stays output only. Data and document often come from different places, and tying the two together would break the common case: 

"1250.5"   { numberSeparators: { decimal: ',', group: '.' } }       -> Total: 1.250,50
"1250.5"   { dataNumberSeparators: { decimal: ',', group: '.' } }   -> TEMPLATE_DATA_INVALID unformattable

Data from a JSON API fills a German document with the first. With one setting for both, it would be refused.

Text That Is a Number

An application filling templates from a table gets every value as text. In 8.6.0, {{ if total > 100 }} with total: '250' was refused as incomparable. In 8.7.0, text that is a number compares with a number as that number, read with dataNumberSeparators when set. Text that is not a number is still refused, because a silent false would pick the wrong branch. With {{ if total > 100 }}Large order{{ else }}Small order{{ endif }}: 

250         -> Large order
"250"       -> Large order
"99.5"      -> Small order
"150 EUR"   -> TEMPLATE_DATA_INVALID incomparable (text with number)
"1.234,50"  -> TEMPLATE_DATA_INVALID incomparable (text with number)
"1.234,50"  -> Large order   (with dataNumberSeparators: { decimal: ',', group: '.' })

A Keyword From Another Language

Template languages spell their branches differently, and a hand used to another one types {{ elseif b }}, {{ elif b }} or {{ end if }}. 8.6.0 already refused these with TEMPLATE_SYNTAX and the remedy in its message. 8.7.0 puts the fix in details.suggestion, the tag as it should be typed, so an editor can offer it: 

{{ elseif b }}   -> TEMPLATE_SYNTAX unreadable, suggestion {{ else if b }}
{{elif  b}}      -> TEMPLATE_SYNTAX unreadable, suggestion {{else if b}}
{{ end if }}     -> TEMPLATE_SYNTAX unreadable, suggestion {{ endif }}

The spaces typed next to the delimiters are kept, so the suggestion matches how the tag was written.

What It Does Not Catch

  • {{ name } } balances, so it is read as code and not reported, though it is likely a typo. A rule that reported it would also report code.
  • A brace stored as a numeric character reference, {, is not counted as a brace.
  • The scan's cost grows with the length of the delimiters, which a caller sets.
  • Across parts, the 1,000 listings fill in the order the parts are compiled, not the order they are shown.

item.title: Reading a Details Block in Markdown the Way GitHub Shows It
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: How officeParser 8.7.0 reads a README's details and summary tags as a disclosure, following CommonMark for blocks and a browser's tree builder for which element an end tag closes, and how it is checked against a reference and a browser.
item.content:encoded:
A README on GitHub often folds its longer parts away behind a triangle. "Building from source", a click, and the steps open. In Markdown that is a few lines of HTML around ordinary Markdown: 

<details>
<summary>Building from source</summary>

Clone the repository, then:

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
```

- Node 18 or later
- No native modules

</details>

Back in the README.

officeParser 8.6.0 read that as text. The summary became a paragraph, the body followed it, and saved back to Markdown the fold was gone, with no warning: 

Building from source

Clone the repository, then:

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
```

- Node 18 or later
- No native modules

Back in the README.

8.7.0 reads it as a disclosure node. This post is about why that is harder than it looks, the rule the Markdown reader now follows, the designs it took to get there, and how I check it.

Neither Parser Alone

Markdown hands HTML to HTML. But a disclosure in a README is not one piece of HTML: it is a tag, then Markdown paragraphs, lists, quotes and code, then another tag.

First CommonMark decides the blocks. The <details> line starts an HTML block (its name is on CommonMark's list of block-level tags), which runs to the next blank line and takes the <summary> line with it. Then come a paragraph, a fenced code block and a list, all Markdown, and then </details>, another HTML block. The renderer passes the two HTML blocks through as written and renders the rest. Nothing in CommonMark says the paragraph is inside anything.

Then a browser builds a tree from that HTML. Its tree builder opens a details element at <details>, and everything after it is a child until </details> closes it. So the disclosure is a fact about the two together: CommonMark decides blocks and containers, and the browser decides which element each end tag closes.

The browser's half has a rule worth knowing. An end tag closes the nearest open element of its name, and every element opened after it. Here a </details> stands inside a quote: 

<details>
<summary>Notes</summary>

> Read this first.
> </details>
> After the disclosure.

CommonMark puts the last two lines in the quote, as one HTML block (it runs to a blank line). The quote opened after the disclosure, so </details> closes the quote too, and "After the disclosure." lands after both. 8.7.0 reads it that way. The tree, then the Markdown it writes back: 

disclosure
  summary
    paragraph
      text "Notes"
  paragraph
    text "Read this first."
paragraph
  text "After the disclosure."
<details>
<summary>Notes</summary>

> Read this first.

</details>

After the disclosure.

What 8.7.0 Reads

The README above, read with parseOffice(buffer, { fileType: 'md' }), gives this tree (each list node is an item, as everywhere in officeParser's AST): 

disclosure
  summary
    paragraph
      text "Building from source"
  paragraph
    text "Clone the repository, then:"
  code "npm ci\nnpm run build"
  list (unordered item)
    text "Node 18 or later"
  list (unordered item)
    text "No native modules"
paragraph
  text "Back in the README."

The Markdown written back is the input again, line for line. Written as HTML, it is a <details> with its <summary>, a paragraph, a <pre> and a <ul> inside it, and EPUB writes it the same way. Other formats have no fold, so every other writer writes the summary in bold and then the body, nothing hidden.

The summary is a node of its own, the disclosure's first child, holding blocks, because a summary can hold more than a line. GitHub shows a heading in a summary when it is written between a <summary> line and a </summary> line with blank lines around it: 

<details open>
<summary>

### Changes in this release

</summary>

Fixes and **new readers**.

</details>
disclosure (open)
  summary
    heading 3
      text "Changes in this release"
  paragraph
    text "Fixes and "
    text "new readers"
    text "."

Written as HTML, the heading stays in the summary:

<details open=""><summary><h3 id="changes-in-this-release">Changes in this release</h3>

</summary>

<p>Fixes and <b>new readers</b>.</p>

</details>

The Rule, Written Down

The Markdown reader now follows one specification, in src/parsers/MarkdownParser.ts: what GitHub shows is a CommonMark renderer's output, read by a browser's tree builder. In practice that is four things.

Blocks are CommonMark's. A line starting with <details, </details or </summary starts an HTML block, which interrupts a paragraph and is never a lazy continuation line. So it ends a quote or list item it is not marked or indented into.

One tag scan per block (analyzeBlock). In an HTML block, tags are read as a browser's tokenizer reads them: every tag of any name, whole, with its quoted attributes, and comments, declarations and the content of elements such as <script> read past. In paragraph text they are read in CommonMark's inline order: backslash escapes, code spans, link destinations and titles, then raw HTML. In code and pipe tables there are none. So a tag's name inside another tag's attribute is not a tag: 

<p title="the <details> element">Disclosures fold content away.</p>

<details>
<summary>Example</summary>

Folded text.

</details>

After.
paragraph
  text "Disclosures fold content away."
disclosure
  summary
    paragraph
      text "Example"
  paragraph
    text "Folded text."
paragraph
  text "After."

One disclosure, not two, and "After." outside it. A code span works the same way: in a body, `</details>` is text, and the disclosure goes on.

One tree pass (planDisclosures). The tags of all the blocks at a level go through one stack, as a browser builds its tree. A start tag opens an element. An end tag closes the nearest open element of its name in scope (a table and its cells bound the scope) and every element opened after it, or is ignored. A quote, a list item and a heading are elements of their block, closed at its end. That is how </details> closes the quote above, and how a </div> closes a disclosure opened inside its div. Each element is pushed once and popped once, and an end tag finds its element from counts of open elements by name, so the pass is linear in the number of tags.

The summary runs to its </summary>. A disclosure's summary is a <summary> that comes first in it, with only white space, blank lines and ignored end tags before it, and it ends at its </summary> wherever that falls, across blocks. What it holds is read as the body is, Markdown where it spans blocks, and becomes the summary node's children.

Nesting is bounded. Disclosures nest 16 deep; a deeper one is flattened into the one holding it: its tags go, its summary and body stay as text, in order. Eighteen nested disclosures, each with a summary and a line of body, read like this: 

disclosures written: 18, deepest disclosure in the tree: 16
texts kept: 36 of 36
--- the 16th disclosure
disclosure
  summary
    paragraph
      text "Level 16"
  paragraph
    text "Body 16."
  paragraph
    text "Level 17"
  paragraph
    text "Body 17."
  paragraph
    text "Level 18"
  paragraph
    text "Body 18."

Three Designs

I did not start with that rule. The git history of this release shows three designs, and each taught me something about the problem. All three were written on the 8.7.0 branch before the release; only the third was ever published.

The first joined pieces. The Markdown reader already joined an HTML table that spans blank lines into one HTML block, with the Markdown pieces between set aside and read on their own afterwards. A disclosure was handled the same way. Simple READMEs worked, but the body was never read as a document: a later line pass still cut the joined block at a <div> line and left placeholders in the output, alignment did not carry from one piece to the next, and an inline <details> in a body paragraph was counted but never opened.

The second read the body as a document of its own: lift a disclosure's blocks out by its tags and read them with the same block reading as the document, nested disclosures too. That structure was sound, and I kept it. What was wrong was underneath. Where tags were was a list of cases, not a definition: it searched for the names details, summary and table with a pattern, so a quoted attribute holding "<details>" was a tag, and a </div> closed nothing. There was no tree builder either. After every close it cut the rest of the block and scanned it again, which took quadratic time on hostile input, and a slice cut after a tag was read as a text of its own, so paragraph text became blocks and a code span's </details> became a real tag. And the summary was a string, so a heading or a link in it was lost.

The third is the one in 8.7.0. It keeps the second's reading and replaces the machinery: one scan per block, one tree pass per level, the cuts applied once, each slice read as what it was in its block, and the summary a node. The specification above was written down during the second design, but its code still worked case by case, and each fix was right about one case and silent about the next. The third was built from the specification, step for step, with a check against it.

Checking It Against a Browser

Examples cannot check a rule like this. So there is a second implementation, test/helpers/disclosureReference.ts, written apart from the reader: a small CommonMark block parser (with GitHub's pipe tables) that renders HTML, then a small HTML tree builder with the rules of the HTML standard that matter here. It is quadratic in places and does not care, because its texts are short.

A generator draws random Markdown that mixes disclosures with quotes, admonitions, lists, headings, tables, fenced and indented code and HTML blocks, with tags in attributes, comments, upper case, enclosing <div> elements and summaries holding blocks. Here is the start of one it drew: 

```
w0 </details>
<details>
```

<details >
<summary>

w1 w2 w3

</summary>

<details title="a>b">
<summary title="s>t">

For each text, the reader's disclosure tree has to be the reference's, and stay so over three round trips through Markdown, with the Markdown settled. The fast test run draws 1,000 texts and the full run three seeds of 10,000. One seed of 1,000, run for this post: 

{
  checked: 987,
  outOfDomain: 13,
  distinct: 1000,
  reasons: {
    'summary not first in its disclosure': 11,
    'disclosure in a list item, heading or cell closed in another block': 2
  },
  mismatches: 0,
  unstable: 0
}

The texts out of its domain are the cases the reader does not follow yet. They are counted, not hidden.

That leaves the question of whether the reference is right. When I first wrote it, I checked its tree builder against a real one: generated cases, the reference's HTML loaded in Chromium from a page served on my own machine, and the browser's tree compared with the reference's. All 1,419 trees were the same. The generator has learned more shapes since, tag names inside attributes, comments and enclosing elements among them, which that comparison did not cover.

Beside it, random ASTs with disclosures are written to Markdown and HTML and read back over several passes with nothing lost, and hostile shapes (closes in nested quotes, unclosed quoted values, long runs of summaries) are each read at a size n and at 4n, to show the time grows in line with the text.

What It Does Not Read Yet

  • A <summary> placed after body content is the summary in a browser. officeParser reads it as a body paragraph, and the disclosure has no summary.
  • A summary no </summary> closes runs to the end of its disclosure in a browser. Here it ends at the end of its block, so the body stays a body and does not become one long summary.
  • A disclosure written inside a Markdown list item (- <details>...), a heading or a pipe table cell is read as that block's text, tags included, as 8.6.0 read it, and written back with the tags escaped. One in an HTML list item is read, and the Markdown writer writes a list item holding a disclosure as HTML so that it reads back. A disclosure opened in a list item and closed in a later block of that item does not pair inside the item.
  • Disclosures nested more than 16 deep are flattened, their text kept.
  • A few of the Markdown reader's block readings from 8.6.0 still differ from CommonMark, such as lines after an HTML block read as Markdown, some lazy lines in list items, and a <summary> line right after a quote line read as the quote's text. The generator keeps them out, and the reference does not model link destinations, raw-text elements or setext headings.

item.title: How a Document Library Is Tested
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: What officeParser 8.7.0's test suite holds and why: committed baselines and fingerprints, round trips that must settle, seeded generators and the references they are checked against, linear-time ratios, budgets tested from both sides, and LibreOffice as a referee.
item.content:encoded:
officeParser reads fourteen file types and writes fifteen output formats, all through the same tree. A change to how Markdown reads a disclosure can move a word in a Word file written from it. A new limit on repeated content can cut a spreadsheet that was fine. So for any change the question is not only whether it works, but what else it touched.

This post is about how the test suite of 8.7.0 answers that. Each kind of test below is a real one from test/, and every number is one I measured on my Mac (an M1 Pro, Node 24) while writing this, or one the repository records. npm test is the gate a change is done by; npm run test:fast is the same chain without the build steps and with the long suites in fast mode, which leaves PDF out and prints a SKIP row for it.

Output a Change Must Not Touch

The oldest layer is baselines. test/parser/baseline holds, for each of the fourteen sample files, its tree as JSON and its text. test/generator/baseline holds 180 files written from those samples, each beside a file of its metrics. The suites compare against them with some tolerance (a text must match exactly, or else in at least 95% of its characters), but the real check is stricter: npm run test:baseline writes them again, and the diff shows every byte that moved. For that to mean anything the output must be reproducible, so the generator suite pins the modification date that packaged formats such as EPUB write into their metadata and onto every zip entry. Its comment says why: while the baselines changed on every run, they were reverted wholesale, and a real change would have gone with the noise.

Fourteen files are not many documents, though. For a change meant to leave a whole area alone, I fingerprint more. Partway through 8.7.0, before I rewrote how Markdown reads <details>, I took 402 Markdown documents with no disclosure in them: the two Markdown test files and 400 drawn from a seeded fuzz of every other block kind. Each one's tree, metadata, Markdown, HTML and text are hashed into one fingerprint. test/helpers/markdownFingerprints.json keeps them as commit 15a4c7ec gave them (one was written again later, for a meant change to how a captioned picture ends its line), and the test fails if one changes. Running it again now: 

kept from 15a4c7ec: 402 fingerprints; now: 402; differ: 0 (374 ms)

The reader has one random value of its own, a token it uses inside HTML tables, so the helper pins Math.random while it reads. Otherwise the same document would give a new fingerprint on every run.

Round Trips That Settle

A writer whose output is read back should keep what it wrote. That is not the same as writing the same bytes twice: writing Markdown, reading it and writing it again can move a space. What must not happen is a word lost, two words run together, or output that never stops changing.

test/helpers/htmlPathRoundTrip.ts draws random list items holding a disclosure and tables with a merged cell, the two that Markdown writes as HTML, and fills them with 25 kinds of node. Every word is named w0, w1, w2 in order, which makes a loss easy to see: a word missing from the text was lost, and one that is there but not standing alone was joined. Each tree is written and read three times; after every pass every word and anchor id must be there, and a fourth write must equal the third. Here is part of one drawn tree's first write: 

<td><ol><li>w3
<p><a href="https://e.x/v">w4</a></p>
<div class="admonition admonition-important" data-type="important"><p><b>w5</b></p>
<p>w6</p></div>

The second write has one space more, after w3. The third is the second, and so is the fourth. That is settling, and it is why the test compares the last passes, not the first two. The helper on 300 trees: 

seed 1: 300 ASTs, 300 distinct, 25 of 25 kinds, 0 lose words, 0 join words, 0 lose anchors, 0 unsettled (1140 ms)

figureLineGenerator.ts and pictureMatrixGenerator.ts do the same for captioned pictures in every container that holds a line. Their tests also assert coverage: that all 54 pairs of configuration and container were drawn, and that more than 95% of the picture documents were distinct.

A Generator That Repeated Itself

That last assertion is there for a reason. Generated documents come from a seeded generator, so a failure can be replayed. The helpers used the C library's linear congruential generator: 

seed = (seed * 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff;

In JavaScript that product is a floating-point number. Once the seed is large it passes 2^53 and loses its low bits, which from seed 1 happens on the second draw. I ran the old formula until a value came back, and the fixed one for a million draws: 

old formula (floating point): { firstRepeatAt: 11155, cycleLength: 10466 }
new formula (Math.imul):      { firstRepeatAt: null, cycleLength: 'none in 1,000,000 draws' }

A cycle of 10,466 values. On the 8.7.0 branch, before the fix, the template engine's new property test drew 200,000 cases from it and passed, on far fewer cases than it said. I counted the distinct cases (delimiters and text) in those 200,000 draws, before and after commit 084c4afd: 

200,000 look-alike cases, old generator: { distinctTexts: 362, distinctCases: 367 }
200,000 look-alike cases, new generator: { distinctTexts: 188142, distinctCases: 197949 }

367 against 197,949, the numbers in that commit's message. The fix multiplies in 32-bit integer arithmetic, Math.imul(seed, 1103515245), which keeps the full period of 2^31, and divides by 2^31 rather than 2^31 minus 1, so an index picked from a draw always falls inside its list.

A property test that passes says nothing about how much it tried, so the generated tests written since print how many of their documents were distinct, and some assert it. The old formula is still in a few places, among them the fingerprint corpus above, whose documents are fixed by the fingerprints kept for them. I counted those too: all 402 are distinct.

Checked Against a Reference

A random document needs an expected answer, and the code under test cannot give it. So two of 8.7.0's readings have a second implementation, plain and slow on purpose, to be checked against.

test/helpers/lookalikeReference.ts is the template engine's look-alike scan, which reports text that looks like a tag but is not one. The engine's scan is built to be fast; the reference keeps braces as objects on a stack and, by its own comment, is quadratic. In Dear {{name}, your {{ order }} and {{total}} it finds one look-alike, {{name}, as missing-delimiter. Each random text is scanned with room to list 0, 1, 2, 3 and 1,000, and the engine must list the reference's first ones and count the rest exactly. Fast mode runs 20,000 texts, the full suite 200,000: 

look-alike scan: 20,000 texts, 10645 with look-alikes, 0 differences (545 ms)

test/helpers/disclosureReference.ts does the same for Markdown disclosures: a small CommonMark block parser, then the HTML standard's tree-building rules that matter here, to say which words each disclosure holds as GitHub shows it. A reference is only useful if it is honest about its edges. Texts the reader does not read as the reference does, some by design and some open findings, are counted as out of its domain and named: 

disclosures: 1,000 texts, 1000 distinct, 987 in the reference's domain, 0 differ, 0 unsettled (2088 ms)
out of domain: {"summary not first in its disclosure":11,"disclosure in a list item, heading or cell closed in another block":2}

Linear Time, Measured as a Ratio

A small file must not cost minutes. The comments in test/security/testSanitization.ts record why that needs saying: a line of backticks or of [x]( once took minutes to read, and 5,000 spaces in a table's delimiter row took 81 seconds.

A limit in seconds does not test this well: a fast machine passes a quadratic loop, a busy one fails a linear one. So the suite's linear helper measures growth. It runs a shape at a quarter of its size, then at full size, and allows the full run eight times the quarter's time plus 250 ms. Linear work takes four times as long; quadratic work takes sixteen; the machine's speed cancels out. A case over the bound is measured once more and the faster times kept, and a full run over two minutes fails whatever its ratio. Three of its Markdown shapes, measured here at the same two sizes: 

200 KB of backticks: 4 ms at a quarter, 11 ms at full size, ratio 2.4, within the bound: true
200 KB of "[x](": 8 ms at a quarter, 27 ms at full size, ratio 3.5, within the bound: true
a table and a line of 200,000 spaces: 5 ms at a quarter, 16 ms at full size, ratio 3.4, within the bound: true

test/helpers/timing.ts sets the rule for the rest: no limit on wall-clock time is checked on a single measurement. The last fix made before the 8.7.0 release, in code new to it, was of this kind: a disclosure summary made only of named anchors looked each id up in the list so far (commit a77ddfbb), and its test now holds 80,000 anchors to eight times the time of 20,000, plus 250 ms.

Budgets and What They Stop

Size is the other cost. A document can refer to the same content many times, and every writer writes it out at each use. decompressionLimits.maxRepeatedContent, 16 MiB by default plus 16 characters for each byte of the document, bounds that. To see what it stops, I built the ODT of headerPartWeightTests: two header parts whose one run has a font name of 50,000 characters, shown by 2,000 paragraphs that alternate between them. I read it with the default budget, then with it lifted: 

the file: 2,007 bytes
default budget: 4000 headers, JSON 9,867,449 characters, 130 ms
   REPEATED_CONTENT_LIMIT_EXCEEDED: Repeated content limit (16809328 characters: decompressionLimits.maxRepeatedContent, plus 16 per byte of the document) reached
repeat budget lifted: 4000 headers, JSON 201,773,622 characters, 315 ms

Two kilobytes that would become 200 MB of JSON. The test asserts that the ODT and DOCX versions warn, stay under three times the budget and still write HTML, and that the same file with a 100-character font, alternated 200 times, keeps every header, unwarned. Running only that function, the ODT half: 

PASS: odt: two headers in a 50,000-character font alternated 2,000 times are charged with the font, with REPEATED_CONTENT_LIMIT_EXCEEDED | REPEATED_CONTENT_LIMIT_EXCEEDED json 9867449, html <!DOCTYPE html>
PASS: odt: two headers in a 100-character font alternated 200 times are all kept, unwarned | 400 headers, 0 empty

That second line matters as much as the first, because a budget that cuts ordinary documents is a bug of its own. In xlsxCellAllowanceTests that is the side that failed. A cell showing a shared string again costs the zip three or four bytes, so a budget growing with the file's bytes grew too little: the comment records 100,000 such cells over 500 rich strings losing the runs of 14,218. That happened on the 8.7.0 branch, after I made each copied value count exactly once; 8.6.0, which counted less, cut none. The fix gives each such cell a small allowance, and the test checks both the ordinary workbooks and the allowance, cell by cell: 

PASS: xlsx: 200,000 cells showing 500 rich strings of four runs again (704 KB) keep every run, unwarned | 200000 cells, 0 cut
PASS: xlsx: 50,000 cells showing a 228-character string are charged 128 less each while 64 characters a byte of the zip last, and no more | 2447 whole, expected 2447 (734 without the allowance) of 50000

The expected 2,447 is not a snapshot: the test works it out from the parser's own constants, so a parser that counts differently fails. Security war stories covers the older limits in this family.

LibreOffice as a Referee

Reading my own output back only proves that my reader agrees with my writer; both can be wrong the same way. An independent program is a better judge, and the repository leans on LibreOffice: the commit that added the ODT writer records that all 13 of its baselines open cleanly in LibreOffice Writer, and the note-number tests encode marks as LibreOffice 7.3 shows them. No test in npm test runs LibreOffice, so I run it by hand. For this post I wrote test.docx as DOCX, ODT and RTF and test.xlsx as XLSX and ODS, had LibreOffice 7.3.7.2 convert each to HTML, and looked for every word of officeParser's own reading in LibreOffice's: 

test.docx written as docx: 11,804 bytes; LibreOffice converted it: true; 416 distinct words in the library's reading, 1 not in LibreOffice's (iii)
test.docx written as odt: 9,193 bytes; LibreOffice converted it: true; 416 distinct words in the library's reading, 1 not in LibreOffice's (iii)
test.docx written as rtf: 54,778 bytes; LibreOffice converted it: true; 416 distinct words in the library's reading, 0 not in LibreOffice's
test.xlsx written as xlsx: 12,331 bytes; LibreOffice converted it: true; 386 distinct words in the library's reading, 0 not in LibreOffice's
test.xlsx written as ods: 6,400 bytes; LibreOffice converted it: true; 387 distinct words in the library's reading, 1 not in LibreOffice's (4000000000000004)

The iii is a list number: in the HTML LibreOffice made from the ODT, that list is <ol type="i" start="3">, so its numbering carries on as the library reads it. The other is a real difference. The sample workbook stores 4.4000000000000004; the library reads those digits, and the ODS writer keeps them as the cell's text beside the value 4.4; LibreOffice shows 4.4. That is what a referee is for: the two readings disagree, and now I know where to look.

What the Suite Does Not Do

AGENTS.md keeps its own list of gaps. There is no coverage floor: tests are written per suite and fixture, not per function. The browser tests of the visualizer exist but are not in the npm test chain. And a fast run says nothing about PDF.

What the suite does have is a habit: for every kind of check, ask how it could pass while proving nothing. A baseline that churns, a generator that cycles, a reference with no stated edges, a time limit that depends on the machine, a budget that cuts ordinary files. Each layer above answers one of those.

item.title: Two Versions of pdf.js in One Process
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why an application's own pdf.js and officeParser's could not read PDFs in the same Node process, why a version range or a peer dependency was not the fix, and how officeParser 8.6.0 gives its pdf.js a worker of its own.
item.content:encoded:
An application renders PDF pages with its own pdf.js, 6.4.299, and extracts their text with officeParser, which uses pdf.js 6.2.108. Both are fine on their own. Together, the second one to read a PDF fails: 

The API version "6.2.108" does not match the Worker version "6.4.299".

That was issue #128. The report asked whether officeParser could take a version range for pdfjs-dist, or make it a peer dependency, so the package manager installs one copy. This post is about why I did neither, what the clash really is, and how 8.6.0 runs two versions of pdf.js side by side in one Node process.

Reproducing It

Two packages in a scratch project: pdfjs-dist@6.4.299 for the application, and officeParser, which brings its own pdfjs-dist@6.2.108. npm installs both copies, one nested under officeParser. The application opens a page first, then asks officeParser for the text: 

import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { getDocument, version } from 'pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.mjs'; // the app's own pdf.js
import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const file = readFileSync('report.pdf');

const doc = await getDocument({ data: new Uint8Array(file) }).promise;
await doc.getPage(1);
console.log(`app's pdf.js ${version}: ${doc.numPages} pages`);

try {
    const ast = await parseOffice(file);
    console.log(`officeParser: ${(await ast.to('text')).value.length} characters of text`);
} catch (error) {
    console.log(`officeParser: ${error.message}`);
}

On officeParser 8.5.0:

app's pdf.js 6.4.299: 8 pages
officeParser: [OfficeParser]: The API version "6.2.108" does not match the Worker version "6.4.299".

The other order fails too, the other way round. With officeParser reading first, in the same process (separateProcess: false), it is the application's pdf.js that breaks: 

officeParser: 9081 characters of text
app's pdf.js 6.4.299: The API version "6.4.299" does not match the Worker version "6.2.108".

One Global for Every Copy

pdf.js comes in two halves: the API you call (getDocument), and a worker that does the parsing. In a browser the worker is a real Web Worker, started from its own file. Node has no Web Workers, so pdf.js runs what it calls a fake worker: the worker's code, in the same thread, talking to the API through a port. To get that code it first looks for a worker someone has already loaded, on a global: 

static get #mainThreadWorkerMessageHandler() {
  try {
    return globalThis.pdfjsWorker?.WorkerMessageHandler || null;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

Only if that is empty does it import the worker file it was told about, and either way it keeps the answer for good. The worker file, as it loads, puts itself on that global: 

globalThis.pdfjsWorker = {
  WorkerMessageHandler: WorkerMessageHandler
};

So the first copy of pdf.js to start a worker in a process names it on globalThis, and every other copy that starts one later finds it there and takes it, whatever its version. Then the worker checks the version of the API talking to it, finds another one, and refuses the document. That is the error.

The two copies on disk are not the problem. Two copies of most packages live side by side without noticing, because each keeps its state in its own modules. pdf.js's worker is shared through the one object every module in the process can see.

Why Not a Range, or a Peer Dependency

A range such as ^6.2.108 would have helped this report. npm would have seen that 6.4.299 fits it and installed one copy for both. But it only helps while the application's version fits the range: an application on 5.x or 7.x still gets two copies, and so does one using another package that brings its own pdf.js. And it hands the choice of officeParser's pdf.js to whatever else is installed.

That matters because what officeParser reads from a PDF depends on pdf.js's output, which changes between releases. Here is getMarkInfo(), which says whether a PDF is tagged, on the same tagged file, in four releases of pdf.js 6:

pdf.jsgetMarkInfo()Page 1 structure tree
6.2.108{"Marked":true,"UserProperties":false,"Suspects":false}1 top node
6.3.289{}1 top node
6.4.299{}1 top node
6.5.438{}1 top node

The structure is still there in every release, but the flag that announces it is gone from 6.3.289 on, in minor releases of the same major version. officeParser decides whether to trust a PDF's tags by that flag, so under a range, the same officeParser on the same file would read headings from the tags in one application and guess them from font sizes in another. When 6.3.289 came out, I tried it and reverted, because six tests of tagged PDFs failed. A peer dependency moves the same choice to every user, and asks each of them to find a version that works.

So pdfjs-dist stays pinned to the version officeParser is tested with. The pin keeps officeParser's output the same for everyone; the clash has to be fixed where it happens.

A Worker of Its Own

In Node, officeParser reads PDFs in a separate process by default, with its own memory limit. That process has a global of its own, so it was never part of the clash. Why did the first sample fail, then? Because 8.5.0 saw the application's worker on the global and took it for one the caller had loaded on purpose, for officeParser to use, and moved the parse into this process to use it. 8.6.0 takes a worker from that global only where pdf.js's worker file cannot be found, which is the case it is there for: a bundle that carries pdf.js inside it.

That leaves parses in this process: with separateProcess: false, or where a process cannot start. There, officeParser now gives its pdf.js a worker module of its own instead of sharing one:

  1. It imports its pdf.js's worker file at the same address with ?officeparser added. Node keeps modules by their full address, query included, so this is a separate instance of the module, even if the application imported the same file.
  2. Loading, that instance puts itself on globalThis.pdfjsWorker, as every copy does. officeParser puts the global back as it was straight away, so the application's pdf.js never sees it.
  3. It connects its pdf.js to that instance through a pair of ports in the same thread, the way pdf.js connects its own fake worker, and gives the API the port. An API given a port uses it and never looks at the global.

Here is a small check of the first two points, with nothing of officeParser in it: 

const plain = await import(workerFile);
const own = await import(`${workerFile}?officeparser`);
console.log('same module object:', plain === own);
console.log('global now names the second copy:', globalThis.pdfjsWorker.WorkerMessageHandler === own.WorkerMessageHandler);
same module object: false
global now names the second copy: true

The second line is why the global has to be put back: left alone, the application's pdf.js would take officeParser's worker from it the next time it started one.

Warnings That Belong to Someone

Sharing a worker also shared its warnings. pdf.js's worker keeps one warning level for every document it reads, in a variable inside its module, which a message can set and nothing can read back. officeParser raises it while it reads a PDF, to report pdf.js's warnings as its own, and 8.4.0 and 8.5.0 left it raised for the application's documents afterwards. With a module of its own, officeParser's level is its own, and the application's worker keeps whatever the application set.

The warnings themselves still arrive through console.warn, which both workers share. To tell its own from the application's, officeParser runs every message its worker receives inside a Node AsyncLocalStorage context, so a warning written anywhere inside that work, after any number of promises and timers, can be traced back to it. The application's warnings, printed outside it, reach the console as they always did.

The Same Script on 8.6.0

app's pdf.js 6.4.299: 8 pages
officeParser: 9081 characters of text

And officeParser first, in the same process:

officeParser: 9081 characters of text
app's pdf.js 6.4.299: 8 pages

Where It Still Shares

A bundle that inlines pdf.js, such as an ESM bundle for Node or an application shipped without node_modules, has no worker file for officeParser to import. There officeParser's own bundled worker goes on the global, and a pdf.js of another version in the same bundle would find it, as before. In that setup, use officeParser's version of pdfjs-dist. In a browser, pdf.js normally starts a real Web Worker from its own file, so the clash needs a worker loaded on the page itself.

And the pin has a cost of its own: officeParser's pdf.js moves only when I move it. The table above is also the plan for that. Before officeParser can take 6.4 or 6.5, it has to read a PDF's tags from the structure tree rather than from a flag that newer releases no longer set.

item.title: Form Fields That Were Never Text: Check Boxes in Word and OpenDocument
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Where Word and LibreOffice keep a form's check boxes, drop-downs and fields, how officeParser 8.6.0 reads them instead of dropping them, and how its PDF engine draws a box no font it has can draw.
item.content:encoded:
A Word form says "Ticked: ☒ Agree". Extract its text with officeParser 8.5.0 and you get "Ticked: Agree", two spaces and no box. A drop-down set to Blue gives nothing at all where Blue was. The answers were dropped, and nothing said so.

I wrote about reading a filled PDF form, where the values are not in the page but in widgets laid over it. Word and OpenDocument files have the same problem in another shape: a check box or a drop-down is not text in the document either. This post is about where each format keeps them, how officeParser 8.6.0 reads them, and how its own PDF writer draws a box no font it has can draw.

Word: A Field With No Result

Word's legacy form fields (the ones under Developer, Legacy Tools) are fields, like a page number. A field is a run marking its start, its instruction, a run marking where its result begins, the result, and a run marking its end. For a text field, the result is the typed value, so text extraction already found it. Here is a check box instead, cut down to what matters: 

<w:r><w:fldChar w:fldCharType="begin">
  <w:ffData>
    <w:name w:val="C1"/>
    <w:checkBox><w:sizeAuto/><w:default w:val="0"/><w:checked/></w:checkBox>
  </w:ffData>
</w:fldChar></w:r>
<w:r><w:instrText> FORMCHECKBOX </w:instrText></w:r>
<w:r><w:fldChar w:fldCharType="separate"/></w:r>
<w:r><w:fldChar w:fldCharType="end"/></w:r>

Between separate and end there is nothing. Word draws the box from the field's data, w:ffData, which sits inside the start marker. A text extractor that reads results reads an empty one. A drop-down is the same: its entries are w:listEntry elements in its data, and its result is empty too.

So officeParser reads the data:

  • A check box is ticked when w:checked says so. A bare <w:checked/> means on, w:val="0" off. Where there is no w:checked, w:default decides, as Word does. A ticked box reads as ☒ and an empty one as ☐: the characters U+2612 and U+2610, the same ones the PDF form post settled on, so a ticked box survives into plain text, a CSV cell or a search index.
  • A drop-down reads as its chosen entry: the one w:result points to, counting from 0, then w:default's, then the first.

OpenDocument: Two Kinds of Form

LibreOffice Writer has two ways to put a check box in a document, and they are stored nothing alike.

The first is Word's legacy fields, kept when LibreOffice opens and saves a Word form. They become field marks, with the state as named parameters: 

<field:fieldmark text:name="__Fieldmark__2_3781684256"
    field:type="vnd.oasis.opendocument.field.FORMCHECKBOX">
  <field:param field:name="Checkbox_Checked" field:value="true"/>
</field:fieldmark>

<field:fieldmark text:name="__Fieldmark__18_3781684256"
    field:type="vnd.oasis.opendocument.field.FORMDROPDOWN">
  <field:param field:name="Dropdown_ListEntry" field:value="Red"/>
  <field:param field:name="Dropdown_ListEntry" field:value="Green"/>
  <field:param field:name="Dropdown_ListEntry" field:value="Blue"/>
  <field:param field:name="Dropdown_Selected" field:value="2"/>
</field:fieldmark>

The second is LibreOffice's own form controls, and here the text holds nothing but a pointer. Where a check box stands in a paragraph, the paragraph has an empty shape naming a control by its id: 

<draw:control text:anchor-type="as-char" draw:name="Shape2"
    svg:width="1.5004in" svg:height="0.2504in" draw:control="control1"/>

The control itself is somewhere else: in office:forms, at the start of the document's body, where a form lists every control it has with its state and its label: 

<form:checkbox form:name="Agree" form:id="control1"
    form:label="I agree" form:current-state="checked"/>
<form:checkbox form:name="News" form:id="control2"
    form:label="Send news" form:state="checked"/>

Those two boxes look alike and are not. form:state is the box's default, the state it returns to when a form is reset; form:current-state is what it shows. "Send news" is ticked by default and shows empty. officeParser reads the current state, so the two read differently, as they look.

Each kind of control has its own attribute for what it shows. Radio buttons have form:current-selected. Text fields have form:current-value. List boxes mark each selected option. A text area keeps its lines as paragraphs, and a date field may store 20240131, digits alone, in files from older releases. A password field is read as one bullet a character, never as the password. Here is a LibreOffice test file on both releases:

Line in the document8.5.08.6.0
Check boxesTerms: and then .Terms: ☒ I agree and ☐ Send news then ☐.
Radio buttonsSize: Size: ☐ Small ☒ Large
Text fieldName: .Name: Jane Doe.
List box, combo box, dateFruit: ; City: ; When: ;Fruit: Apple, Cherry; City: Berlin; When: 2024-01-31;

Because a control is named, not written, one control can be named many times. A small file can name one long text area thousands of times, and every writer would write it out each time. officeParser reads each control once and shows it whole the first time; every later naming is a single run with its line breaks as spaces, and counts toward decompressionLimits.maxRepeatedContent, the budget for content a document repeats by reference.

Drawing a Box No Font Has

Reading the boxes was half of it. officeParser also writes PDFs, and its native engine draws text in the fonts it is given, or in the PDF's built-in Helvetica and Courier when it is given none. Those fonts have no ☐. Here is a line with all three boxes, written to PDF and read back, on 8.5.0: 

warning: CONTENT_NOT_REPRESENTABLE | The 'non-WinAnsi characters (native engine)' content has no faithful representation in pdf output ...
read back: Plan: ? Basic ? Premium ? Done

8.6.0 adds a font of its own when a box has no other font to draw it: a Type 3 font, the kind of PDF font whose glyphs are drawing instructions instead of an outline file. It has three glyphs, an empty, a ticked and a crossed box, each a square and its mark as filled paths in the text's colour, and a heavier set for bold text. Its ToUnicode map gives each glyph its character, so the box copies and searches as ☐, ☑ or ☒: 

read back: Plan: ☐ Basic ☒ Premium ☑ Done
pdftotext: Plan: ☐ Basic ☒ Premium ☑ Done

The second line is Poppler's pdftotext, which reads PDFs without pdf.js. It needed one more glyph. Poppler works out the size of a Type 3 font's text from the width of the font's first glyph, and with a box first it took the boxes for text 1.6 times their size, set on a line apart from the words around them. A space, half an em wide and never drawn, placed first in the font, fixed that.

What It Does Not Read Yet

  • A control placed inside a drawn shape's text, a rectangle or a custom shape, is still dropped. In a frame it is read.
  • LibreOffice Calc's form controls, in a spreadsheet, are not read.
  • A button reads as nothing, though it shows its label.

item.title: Text That Looks Real: A PDF Font With No Map
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why a PDF line that says "Hi there" can extract as +LWKHUH with no error, why the file cannot always tell you, and what officeParser's PDF_FONT_UNMAPPED warning reports and misses.
item.content:encoded:
Extract the text of some PDFs and a line that says "Hi there" on screen comes out as +LWKHUH. There is no error and nothing is missing: the right number of letters, on the right line, in the right place. It just isn't what the page says, and nothing in the string tells you so.

This post is about why that happens, why the file cannot always tell you, and what officeParser 8.5.0 does about it: a warning, PDF_FONT_UNMAPPED, that names the font and its pages. It also says what the warning misses, because a caller may throw text away on it.

Codes, Glyphs and Characters

A PDF does not store text as characters. A page's content stream draws codes in a font: 

BT /F1 12 Tf 72 700 Td <002B004C00030057004B004800550048> Tj ET

To draw, a viewer only needs to turn each code into a glyph, a shape in the font. A code with no meaning beyond "shape number 43" draws perfectly. To read, something has to say which character that shape is, and that is the job of a font's /ToUnicode map. It is optional, because a page looks the same without it.

The font that breaks is a composite one with the encoding /Identity-H, whose two-byte codes are simply glyph numbers, and no /ToUnicode: 

<< /Type /Font /Subtype /Type0 /BaseFont /ABCDEF+Arial
   /Encoding /Identity-H /DescendantFonts [6 0 R] >>

With nothing to go on, pdf.js reads each code as the character of that number. I embedded Arial this way and drew "Hi there" in its glyph numbers. In Arial, "H" is glyph 0x2B, and 0x2B is "+". The letters are all 29 places out, so "i" becomes "L" and "t" becomes "W". That is the whole of +LWKHUH. In a font that was renumbered when it was subset, the numbers follow no pattern at all.

The Character That Gave It Away

The space in that line is glyph 3, and code 3 reads as U+0003, a control character. Up to 8.2.0, officeParser left it in, so the line read +L\u0003WKHUH. Someone reading that could see something was wrong, and as issue #127 reported, a program could too: it dropped lines with such characters and told its user the page could not be decoded.

In 8.3.0 I took those characters out of all PDF text. PDFs from Chromium and LibreOffice leave stray control characters where a mapping was lost, and they have no place in text. That was right for those files, but it took away the one sign the broken ones gave, and it was never mentioned in the changelog. Twelve lines of such a font in 8.2.0 raised PDF_TEXT_ENCODING_SUSPECT, at 40% of characters unmappable. Since 8.3.0 they raise nothing of the kind, because the characters it counts have gone before it counts them.

A simple font can fall back to its code's own character too, but there the glyph's name can still say what it is. That is another post, and an open report with pdf.js. A composite font on /Identity-H has no such names to read.

Why the File Cannot Just Say

The obvious fix is to look at the font: no /ToUnicode on an Identity encoding, so warn. I started there. These are all the same dictionary but for its name and the codes drawn:

The fontCodes drawnReads as
Arial, embeddedArial's glyph numbers+LWKHUH
Named Arial, not embeddedArial's glyph numbersHi there
Any name, not embeddedUnicode code pointsHi there

In the second row pdf.js knows Arial's numbers by its name, so the codes are mapped after all, and that case can be told from the glyphs pdf.js returns. The third is harder. A producer can simply use Unicode code points as its glyph numbers. Tesseract's text layer does: I removed the /ToUnicode from a Tesseract PDF, and its text came out exactly the same. A warning on the structure alone would call that text garbage, and a caller who drops text on the warning would lose it.

So the control characters are not just the old symptom. They are the evidence. Real words in real characters don't have U+0003 in them, and text in low glyph numbers, where the space is glyph 3 as it is in Arial, does.

The Rule

A font is reported only when all of these hold:

  • Control characters were taken out of text in that font that stays in the output. Glyphs an /ActualText replaces don't count, since what they stand for is what you get.
  • It has readable text, not only blanks.
  • On every page with its text, its glyphs were seen and every one read as its own code. A page whose operators were cut short by a limit can't say, so the font is not reported.
  • Its dictionary is a composite font on an Identity encoding with no /ToUnicode stream.

The last check has to find a font's dictionary, and pdf.js gives a font's name but not its dictionary. My first version matched them by following the order fonts are set in each page's content. That read content streams the parser otherwise had no reason to read, and they spend the same bounded budget that reads /ActualText. On a long file, a warning changed the text of a later page. Now the judgement runs after every page is read, finds the font by name in the page's resources, and reads no content at all. A warning has no business changing what it warns about.

Using It

The warning comes once for each font name, with every page that has its text. A text run carries the same name, so you can find the lines themselves: 

import { parseOffice } from "officeparser";
import { readFile } from "fs/promises";

const ast = await parseOffice(await readFile(process.argv[2]));

for (const warning of ast.warnings) {
    if (warning.code !== "PDF_FONT_UNMAPPED") continue;
    console.log(warning.details.font, warning.details.pages);
}

const unmapped = new Set(ast.warnings
    .filter(warning => warning.code === "PDF_FONT_UNMAPPED")
    .map(warning => warning.details.font));
const readable = node => node.children
    ? node.children.map(readable).join("")
    : unmapped.has(node.formatting?.font) ? "" : node.text ?? "";
console.log(ast.content.map(readable).join("\n"));

On a page with one good line and the Arial line above, that prints: 

Arial [ 1 ]
A line that decodes

The text itself is left as it was. Whether to drop it, flag it or send the page to OCR is your call.

What It Misses

The rule prefers saying nothing to being wrong, so it stays quiet on a good deal of garbage:

  • No control character, no warning. If no code of the font falls in that range, as in a subset renumbered from higher up, the line reads ŵŶŝ and nothing is said. The same was true in 8.2.0. This is the biggest gap: I would rather read the embedded font and confirm the codes are glyph numbers, which is work for a later release.
  • PDF_TEXT_ENCODING_SUSPECT still does not count these characters. Counting them brought it back, along with false alarms on good prose in a font with no entry for its space, so it stays as it has been since 8.3.0 for now.
  • Encrypted files and files my reader cannot follow get no warning, because the font's dictionary is out of reach. Nor do fonts on an embedded CMap, or two fonts of one name on every page.
  • It can be wrong the other way. A font of Unicode codes with a stray control character among them is reported, which is why the message says "likely".

A warning that is sometimes silent is still useful, as long as it says what it knows and you don't read its silence as a guarantee. If a document matters, compare a page of its text with the page itself.

item.title: The Answer Was in the Glyph's Name: When "nicht" Reads "ni!ht"
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why a word a PDF draws correctly can read "ni!ht" in pdf.js, what the Adobe Glyph List's rules say a name like c.sc means, how officeParser reads it, and the report I filed with pdf.js.
item.content:encoded:
A page says nicht The café. Search for "nicht" in the PDF.js viewer and it says "Phrase not found". Search for "ni!ht" and it finds the word the page shows as "nicht". The drawing is right and the text behind it is wrong, and the answer is sitting in the file, in the name of the glyph.

I touched on this in the post on filled forms, where it turned up. This post is the whole of it: how a name can say what a glyph is, why the text comes out wrong without it, how officeParser reads it since 8.4.1, and the report I filed with pdf.js so that everyone using it can get the right text.

A File Small Enough to Read

I built one page with one font, an embedded subset with no /ToUnicode and this encoding: 

<< /Type /Encoding /BaseEncoding /WinAnsiEncoding
   /Differences [33 /c.sc 34 /T_h.alt 35 /uni00E9.sc] >>

The content stream draws the bytes ni!ht "e caf#. Most of those codes mean what WinAnsi says. The three in /Differences select glyphs by name instead: code 33, which WinAnsi calls "!", draws the font's glyph named c.sc, a small capital c. So the page shows the right word.

Reading it is a separate question. Here is pdf.js 6.2.108, the version officeParser uses, on that file: 

import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { getDocument } from 'pdfjs-dist/legacy/build/pdf.mjs';

const data = new Uint8Array(readFileSync('glyph-name-suffix.pdf'));
const doc = await getDocument({ data }).promise;
const text = await (await doc.getPage(1)).getTextContent();
console.log(JSON.stringify(text.items.map((i) => i.str).join('')));
"ni!ht \"e caf#"

With no name it knows and no map, each code falls back to its own character. Those are the bytes of the content stream, read as text.

What a Name Says

Glyph names look like private labels, but they aren't. The Adobe Glyph List specification gives rules for turning a name into text, so that software can do exactly this:

  1. Drop everything from the first period on. It is a variant's suffix: c.sc is c.
  2. Split the rest at underscores. They join the parts of a ligature: T_h is T and h.
  3. Read each part: a name in the list, or uniXXXX, or uXXXX up to six digits.
  4. The text is the parts in order.

So c.sc is "c", T_h.alt is "Th", and uni00E9.sc is "é". The specification even recommends names like these for new fonts, so suffixes are open-ended: c.alt, one.osf and A.swash all work the same way. A list of known names can never cover them, but the rule does.

pdf.js looks a name up whole, and knows some ligatures by name, such as T_h. It doesn't apply the rule, so c.sc and T_h.alt and uni00E9.sc get no mapping. Poppler does apply it, and pdftotext reads that file as nicht The café.

Where It Came From

I found this in an official German form, saved through macOS's Quartz, where "Nein, trifft nicht zu" read "Nein, trifft ni!ht zu". The blank form names the same glyph and gives its code a map entry: to a capital C, so it reads "niCht", which is the file's own doing. Quartz rewrites the subset's encoding and leaves that code out of its map.
