War Story 3: A Few Hundred Bytes, Millions of Cells

OpenDocument has an attribute for compressing runs of identical cells: 

<table:table-row>
  <table:table-cell><text:p>Start</text:p></table:table-cell>
  <table:table-cell table:number-columns-repeated="1048576"/>
</table:table-row>

It exists for a good reason. LibreOffice routinely writes table:number-rows-repeated="1048566" to say "the rest of the sheet is empty". But a parser that takes the number at its word runs this: 

for (let i = 0; i < repeated; i++) {
    row.cells.push(new Cell());
}

Rows repeat too, and the two multiply. The ZIP limits cannot help, because the XML is tiny and the expansion happens later, while the tree is being built. officeParser expanded these attributes without a bound, so a few hundred bytes could ask for millions of nodes. After I fixed that for sheets, the same attribute turned up in a chart's embedded table: a 1.3 KB document that repeated one cell 100,000,000 times ended the process out of memory.

The fix could not be "cap the attribute", because that breaks real spreadsheets. What is bounded instead is what gets built:

  • A document may materialize at most maxTableCells cells (default 1,000,000, plus one for each byte of the file, so a large real spreadsheet is not cut short). Past that the parser clamps and warns once.
  • A repeated empty cell builds nothing and is skipped in one step. Looping over it was a CPU attack of its own.
  • Repeated rows and columns share their child nodes; they are not deep copies.
  • maxRepeatedContent (default 16,777,216 characters, plus 16 for each byte of the file) bounds the total content a document may repeat by reference.

War Story 4: Nesting That Runs the Stack Out

XML lets elements nest, and an attacker can nest the same element thousands deep: 

<w:p>
  <w:hyperlink>
    <w:hyperlink>
      <w:hyperlink>
        ... thousands of levels ...
      </w:hyperlink>
    </w:hyperlink>
  </w:hyperlink>
</w:p>

This one bit twice. The first problem was time. Every level of nested hyperlink applied its link to every run inside it, so the work grew with depth times runs. A 23 KB file with 1,000 levels around 400,000 runs took 17 seconds. Now the outermost hyperlink applies its link once.

The second problem was the call stack. A recursive reader that goes deep enough throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, and until 8.1.0 that surfaced as a generic "file corrupted" error. How deep is "deep enough" is not a constant. It depends on the engine, the stack size, and even on whether the code has been optimized yet. On Node 25 I measured this traversal running out somewhere between 900 and 1,000 levels in a fresh process.

The 512-level guard

Since 8.1.1 the Word parser counts depth inside a paragraph and stops at 512 levels, well before the stack is at risk. HTML has had a 256-level cap since 7.4.0, and RTF since 8.1.0. Other deep nesting, such as tables inside table cells, still relies on catching the stack overflow. Either way the caller gets the same typed error: 

try {
    await parseOffice(upload);
} catch (err) {
    if (err.officeIssue?.code === 'MAX_NESTING_DEPTH_EXCEEDED') {
        // The input was built to be deep. Reject it.
    }
}

The Baseline, and Its Limits

Beyond those four stories, this is what the library does as a matter of course:

  • Every generator escapes what it writes. Document text is attacker-controlled, so each output has its own escaping: HTML and CSS, URLs, RTF control words, LaTeX commands, Markdown, and CSV formulas.
  • Limits apply to real work, not declared sizes: inflated bytes, ZIP entries, table cells, XML elements, and repeated content.
  • Prototype pollution is closed. A list id of __proto__ in a crafted document once reached Object.prototype through a counter map. Those maps now have no prototype, and the keys __proto__, constructor, and prototype are never copied from a caller's config.
  • The security suite has more than 1,200 checks in test/security/testSanitization.ts. It is part of npm test, which CI runs on every push to master and on every pull request against it.

None of that is a guarantee. I am the sole maintainer, and a parser this size has attack surface I have not found yet. If you process untrusted files, run the parse somewhere you can afford to lose: a worker or container with memory and time limits and low privileges. Use decompressionLimits and abortSignal. Do not rely on any one library's hardening as your whole defence.

item.title: From String Scraping to AST: The Architectural Evolution of officeParser
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why returning one flat string hit a ceiling, and how a typed AST made conversion between Office, Markdown, HTML, and LaTeX possible.
item.content:encoded:
Every library starts with a narrow problem. I wrote the first version of officeParser in 2019 to do one thing: get the text out of Word and PowerPoint files in Node.js, with no LibreOffice to install, no Python to spawn, and no Java bridge.

That first version did exactly that and nothing more. It unzipped the file, parsed document.xml, collected every piece of text it found, and joined the pieces with spaces. You got one flat string.

It was small and it solved the immediate need. Excel and OpenDocument support followed within a week. For years, a flat string was the whole product. Then documents started feeding search indexes and language models, and the flat string became a dead end.

What a Flat String Loses

Consider what happens when you reduce a financial report or a contract to one string:

  • Tables collapse. The cells of a five-column balance sheet become a run of numbers, and which number belonged to which row and column is gone.
  • The outline disappears. A chapter title looks the same as a bullet point three levels down.
  • Links and references vanish. A hyperlink keeps its words and loses its target. A footnote lands wherever the file happened to store it.
  • Code and math lose their edges. Nothing marks where a formula starts or stops.
Why this matters more with LLMs

A language model leans on structure: headings, lists, and tables tell it what belongs together. Hand it a table flattened into a line of numbers and it has to guess which figure answers the question. The information was in the document. The extraction threw it away.

The Pivot: Documents as Compilers See Them

The way out was to stop treating this as a string problem and treat it as a compiler problem.

A compiler does not translate source code to machine code with search and replace. It parses the source into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) that captures what the program means, independent of how it was written down.

Documents work the same way. A table may be written as WordprocessingML (<w:tbl>), OpenDocument (<table:table>), HTML (<table>), Markdown (| col |), or LaTeX (\begin{tabular}). The thing being described is the same every time: rows of cells.

The Shape of the Tree

Version 6 (January 2026) replaced the string with a tree. Every parser returns the same structure: 

OfficeParserAST
├── type         'docx' | 'pptx' | 'pdf' | 'md' | ... (14 formats)
├── metadata     title, author, created, modified, ...
├── content      OfficeContentNode[]
├── auxiliary    headers, footers, slide masters, PDF outline
├── attachments  images and charts (with extractAttachments)
├── warnings     non-fatal issues found while parsing
└── to(format)   generate another format from this tree

Each content node has a type, its text, its children, and optional formatting and metadata. The node types are a closed set: 

type OfficeContentNodeType =
    | 'paragraph' | 'heading' | 'list' | 'text' | 'break' | 'code'
    | 'table' | 'row' | 'cell'
    | 'image' | 'chart' | 'drawing' | 'embed'
    | 'slide' | 'sheet' | 'page' | 'slideMaster'
    | 'note' | 'comment' | 'header' | 'footer'
    | 'admonition'
    | 'definitionList' | 'definitionTerm' | 'definitionDescription';

A table is always table, then row, then cell, whichever format it came from. Footnotes and speaker notes hang off the node that refers to them (node.notes), and so do comments (node.comments).

Hub and Spoke: Why Generation Came Next

Once every format parses into one tree, conversion stops being a matrix. Without a shared tree, converting between formats means writing a translator for every pair: 

DOCX -> Markdown     PPTX -> Markdown
DOCX -> HTML         PDF  -> HTML
ODT  -> DOCX         ... one per pair

With the tree in the middle, each format needs at most two pieces: a parser that produces the tree and a generator that consumes it. 

DOCX   PPTX   PDF   Markdown   LaTeX
   \     |     |      |        /
    v    v     v      v       v
        [ OfficeParserAST ]
    /    |     |      |       \
   v     v     v      v        v
DOCX   HTML   PDF   Markdown   chunks

Version 7.0 (May 2026) added the generators, the chunker for retrieval pipelines, and parsers for Markdown, HTML, and CSV. Version 8.0 added native DOCX and ODT output and a PDF engine that needs no browser. Version 8.1 added LaTeX in both directions. Version 8.3 added XLSX, ODS, PPTX and ODP output. (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: XLSX, ODS, PPTX and ODP output took the outputs from 11 to 15.)

Today that is 14 input formats and 1115 (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: XLSX, ODS, PPTX and ODP output took the outputs from 11 to 15.) outputs. Pair by pair, it would be 154210 (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: XLSX, ODS, PPTX and ODP output took the outputs from 11 to 15.) converters. With the tree, it is 14 parsers and 1115 (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: XLSX, ODS, PPTX and ODP output took the outputs from 11 to 15.) generators, and a new parser can be written to every existing output on the day it lands.

The Round-Trip Rule

Generation brought a rule I now hold every feature to:

A feature is not done until it round-trips

What a parser captures, the matching generator must be able to write back. The test suite checks it directly: parse a sample, generate the same format from the tree, parse the result, and compare what the two trees hold.

That rule is about one format at a time. Across formats, conversion is only as lossless as the target allows. Markdown has no merged cells, so a table with spans is written as an HTML table inside the Markdown. Plain text has no links. Where a target cannot say something, the generator falls back to the closest thing it can say.

Holding to the rule surfaced a long list of details that a text extractor never has to care about:

  • Merged cells (rowSpan, colSpan) surviving between Word, OpenDocument, and HTML tables.
  • List numbering that keeps counting when a list is interrupted by an ordinary paragraph.
  • Bookmarks and heading anchors (anchorIds), so internal links still land.
  • Guarding formula characters in CSV output without corrupting cells that are just negative numbers.

No Office Suite Required

One constraint from 2019 is still in place: parsing needs nothing but the npm package. There is no LibreOffice, no Java, and no Python behind it.

Parsing is JavaScript all the way down. PDF reading uses pdf.js, and OCR uses Tesseract compiled to WebAssembly. That is also why the same code runs in a browser, from a bundle of about 5.5 MB6 MB (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: The browser bundle was about 5.5 MB when this post went out, and grew to about 6 MB with this release.), so a file can be parsed without leaving the user's machine.

There is one place where I traded that purity for fidelity, and it is opt-out. The default PDF output engine renders through headless Chromium (Puppeteer, an optional peer dependency), because a browser's layout engine gives the most faithful page. If you do not want a browser, the native engine writes PDF directly with pdf-lib, with simpler layout and the standard PDF fonts, in the standard PDF fonts or in fonts you give it (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.2.0: The native engine now also draws in TrueType and OpenType fonts you give it, for any script.).

Trade-off Wrapping an office suite officeParser
Install System packages, fonts, and a process to manage One npm package
Runs in the browser No Yes
Page layout fidelity High: it runs a real layout engine Structure, not pixels
What you get back A converted file A typed tree you can inspect, filter, and convert

The third row is a real cost. Where officeParser is the wrong tool covers it and the other jobs this design does not do.

Looking Back

Moving from a string to a tree was not a refactor. It changed what the library is for. Reading a .docx, turning Markdown into a Word report, and chunking a PDF for retrieval look like three features. They are one tree with different things attached to each end.

item.title: Where officeParser is the Wrong Tool: An Honest Engineering Guide
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: The jobs officeParser does not do: PDFs that match Word exactly, formula recalculation, legacy .doc files, formulas and native charts in what it writes, macros, and TeX typesetting, and what to use instead.
item.content:encoded:
Every architecture is a set of trade-offs. When I designed officeParser, I made three on purpose:

  • I chose an npm package with no office suite behind it over wrapping a desktop application.
  • I chose structure and meaning over reproducing how a page looks in print.
  • I chose running in both Node.js and the browser over features that would need a native rendering engine.

Those choices make officeParser a good fit for document ingestion, format conversion, and client-side processing. They also mean there are jobs it cannot do, and it is better that you hear that from me than discover it in production.

If your project needs any of the following, use something else.

1. You Need a PDF That Matches Word Exactly

Suppose the requirement is: "I have a contract in Word. I need a PDF with the same line breaks and the same page breaks that Word would produce."

officeParser cannot do this.

Where Word breaks a line or a page is not written in the file. It is computed by Word's layout engine from font metrics, kerning, and its own rules. officeParser models what a document says: headings, paragraphs, tables, lists, formatting. Its PDF output lays that structure out again, through a browser engine or its own simpler one. The content will be right. The page breaks will not be Word's.

What to use instead
  • Word itself, or Microsoft's own conversion through the Graph API. Only Word's engine reproduces Word.
  • LibreOffice in headless mode: soffice --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx. Close to Word, though not identical, and it needs the document's fonts installed.
  • Gotenberg: a Docker service that wraps LibreOffice and Chromium behind an HTTP API.

2. You Need a Spreadsheet That Recalculates

Suppose the requirement is: "Load a workbook, change cell B4, and have every formula that depends on it update."

officeParser is not a calculation engine.

When it reads an .xlsx file, it reads the values: for a formula cell, the result Excel computed and saved the last time the file was written. It does not read the formula text, it does not evaluate anything, and it cannot write an .xlsx back out and it does not evaluate anything, so an .xlsx it writes back out holds the values, not the formulas (Updated 28 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: officeParser now writes .xlsx files, with each cell's value and not its formula.) (see section 4).

What to use instead
  • HyperFormula: a headless spreadsheet engine in TypeScript, from the Handsontable team, with a dependency graph and several hundred built-in functions.
  • ExcelJS: reads and writes workbooks, including formulas and styling. It does not calculate either.
  • Apache POI (Java): workbook manipulation with a formula evaluator.

3. You Have Legacy Binary Files (.doc, .xls, .ppt)

The pre-2007 Office formats are a different family: binary records inside a compound file, not XML in a ZIP. officeParser reads the modern formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx), OpenDocument, PDF, RTF, and the text formats. It does not read .doc, .xls, or .ppt.

If you have an archive of old files, convert them first. LibreOffice does this well: soffice --headless --convert-to docx old-file.doc. Then parse the result.

4. You Need to Write Spreadsheets or SlidesFormulas or Native Charts in the Files You Write (Updated 26 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: officeParser now writes .xlsx, .ods, .pptx and .odp files, so this section is now about what those files leave out.)

officeParser reads fourteen formats but writes fewer. It generates DOCX, ODT, PDF, HTML, Markdown, LaTeX, RTF, EPUB, CSV, plain text, and chunks for retrieval. It does not generate .xlsx, .pptx, .ods, or .odp. Since 8.3.0, officeParser writes spreadsheets and slides as well as documents: .xlsx, .ods, .pptx and .odp, next to DOCX, ODT, PDF, HTML, Markdown, LaTeX, RTF, EPUB, CSV, plain text and chunks for retrieval. What it writes is what it read: a workbook's values, shown in their number formats, and a deck's text boxes, pictures, shapes, tables and speaker notes. (Updated 26 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: officeParser now writes .xlsx, .ods, .pptx and .odp files, so this section is now about what those files leave out.)

A spreadsheet can go out as CSV, and a deck can go out as a document, but if the deliverable has to open in Excel or PowerPoint as a native file, use a library built for writing them, such as ExcelJS or PptxGenJS. It does not write formulas, since it never reads them (see section 2), and it writes a chart as a table of its data, on a sheet or a slide, not as a chart Excel or PowerPoint can edit. If the deliverable needs live formulas or editable charts, use a library built for authoring them, such as ExcelJS or PptxGenJS. (Updated 26 Oct 2026 for 8.3.0: officeParser now writes .xlsx, .ods, .pptx and .odp files, so this section is now about what those files leave out.)

5. You Need to Run Macros

Macro-enabled files carry VBA code. officeParser has no VBA runtime. It never executes macro code, and it does not read it or carry it into anything it generates. If your workflow depends on a macro running, you need Office itself.

6. You Need a TeX Engine

officeParser reads LaTeX and writes LaTeX, but it interprets LaTeX. It does not compile it.

Reading a .tex file, it follows the structure the way a converter does: sections, lists, tables, math, footnotes, citations, and the macros you define yourself (\newcommand, \def), which it expands within fixed limits. It does not load packages, so a command from a package it does not know keeps its text. Drawings (TikZ, pgfplots, picture) are left out. And it never typesets, so there are no line breaks, page numbers, or floats placed on a page.

Going the other way, ast.to('tex') gives you source that compiles with pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, or LuaLaTeX. To turn that source into a camera-ready PDF, you still run a real TeX distribution.

Smaller Limits Worth Knowing

  • Slide reading order. Shapes on a slide are read in the order the file lists them, not sorted by position. The PPTX article explains why that is hard.
  • Untagged PDFs. Without a tag tree, tables and headings are recovered from geometry, which is best-effort. The PDF article has the details.
  • Runtime. The npm package needs Node.js 22.13 or newerNode.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 or later in its line (Updated 1 Nov 2026 for 8.5.0: Earlier Node.js releases have a flaw in their Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497), so the package now asks for one with the fix.).

The Decision Matrix

A summary of how officeParser compares with three tools people often reach for:

Capability officeParser Pandoc LibreOffice (headless) python-docx / openpyxl
What you install An npm package A native binary A full office suite Python packages
Runs in the browser Yes Not as shipped Not as shipped Not as shipped
One document model across formats Yes (typed AST) Yes (Pandoc AST) Only through its UNO API No, one model per library
Chunks for retrieval Built in No No No
Legacy .doc / .xls / .ppt No No Yes No
Formula recalculation No No Yes No
Print layout close to Word No No Closest of the four No

When officeParser is the Right Tool

Reach for it when the job is:

  • Getting documents into a search index, a retrieval pipeline, or an LLM prompt with their structure intact.
  • Converting between Office formats, Markdown, HTML, LaTeX, and PDF from one typed tree.
  • Processing documents in the browser, so a confidential file never leaves the user's machine.
  • Running in a plain Node.js service where you would rather not install and supervise an office suite.

That is the job it was built for. For everything above the line, use the tool built for that job. Knowing where the boundary sits is part of using any library well.

item.title: Document Chunking for Retrieval Done Right: Beyond Naive Token Windows
item.dc:creator: Harsh Ankur
item.description: Why a sliding token window shreds tables and orphans headings, what chunking on document structure fixes, and what officeParser's chunker does and does not do.
item.content:encoded:
In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the quality of the answer is bounded by the quality of what was retrieved. If the relevant passage never reaches the context window, no amount of prompt engineering will produce it.

Yet a great many pipelines still ingest documents with some variation of this: 

// The usual first attempt:
const text = extractRawText(file);
const chunks = recursiveTextSplitter(text, {
    chunkSize: 500,
    chunkOverlap: 50,
});

For prose this is tolerable. For office documents, with their tables and nested headings, it loses exactly the parts that matter. Here is why.

The Anatomy of Chunking Failure

A window of fixed size sliding over a string is blind to structure. It cuts wherever the count runs out:

1. The Table Shredder

Take a financial table with a header row and a row per quarter. The window fills up partway through, and the splitter cuts there:

  • Chunk 1 holds the header row and the first three quarters.
  • Chunk 2 starts with: | Q4 | 47,310 | 19.0% |.

Chunk 2 has lost its column names. When someone asks "What was the operating margin in Q4?", the words "operating margin" appear only in chunk 1, so chunk 2 is a poor match for the query. And if it is retrieved anyway, the model has no way to know what 19.0% measures.

2. The Orphaned Heading

A heading is the context for everything under it. A fixed window often leaves the heading at the end of one chunk and its content at the start of the next: 

[End of chunk 24]
... in accordance with regional regulations.
4.2 Data Retention Exceptions

[Start of chunk 25]
Medical records must be archived for a minimum of 7 years.
All audit trails must be immutable.

Retrieve chunk 25 alone and nothing says that "7 years" is about data retention exceptions and not about, say, ordinary log storage.

The Fix: Chunk the Structure, Not the String

Both failures come from the same place: by the time the splitter runs, the structure is already gone. The fix is to chunk before flattening, while a table is still a table and a heading is still a heading.

Three rules for structural chunking
  1. Cut at structural boundaries. Between paragraphs, sections, pages, or slides. Never in the middle of a table row.
  2. Carry the heading. Every chunk should know which heading it sits under, ideally the whole path of headings above it.
  3. Repeat table headers. When a table is too big for one chunk, every piece should start with the header row.

What officeParser's Chunker Does

officeParser parses every format into one tree, so its chunker works on nodes, not characters. You reach it with ast.to('chunks'): 

import { parseOffice } from 'officeparser';

const ast = await parseOffice('service-agreement.docx');

const { value: chunks } = await ast.to('chunks', {
    chunksConfig: {
        strategy: 'document-structure',  // the default
        splitBy: 'heading',  // or 'paragraph', 'page', 'slide', 'sheet'
        maxChunkSize: 1500,
        tableSplitStrategy: 'row',       // repeat the header row
    },
});

Here is real output for a short Markdown document: a paragraph under the heading "3.2 Uptime Credits", followed by a four-row table that I forced to split by setting a small maxChunkSize. The chunks for the headings themselves are left out: 

[
  {
    "text": "If monthly uptime falls below 99.9%, the customer is
             entitled to a 10% credit. Below 99.0%, a 25% credit
             applies.",
    "metadata": {
      "sourceType": "md",
      "closestHeading": "3.2 Uptime Credits"
    }
  },
  {
    "text": "| Quarter | Revenue | Operating margin |
             | Q1 | 41,900 | 16.2% |
             | Q2 | 43,750 | 17.1% |
             | Q3 | 45,200 | 18.4% |",
    "metadata": {
      "sourceType": "md",
      "closestHeading": "3.2 Uptime Credits",
      "isTableChunk": true
    }
  },
  {
    "text": "| Quarter | Revenue | Operating margin |
             | Q4 | 47,310 | 19.0% |",
    "metadata": {
      "sourceType": "md",
      "closestHeading": "3.2 Uptime Credits",
      "isTableChunk": true
    }
  }
]

(The long strings are wrapped here to fit the page.) Measured against the three rules:

  • Rule 1, boundaries: done, with one exception. Chunks follow the tree, and a table is cut between rows. A single row longer than maxChunkSize is cut inside, because no chunk could hold it whole.
  • Rule 3, table headers: done. The second table chunk begins with the header row, so the Q4 figures still have their column names. isTableChunk marks both pieces.
  • Rule 2, headings: partly. Each chunk records its closestHeading, along with pageNumber, slideNumber, or sheetName where the format has them. But it is the nearest heading only, not the full path above it, and it lives in the metadata, not in the text that gets embedded.

Putting the Heading Where the Embedding Can See It

If the heading is only in metadata, the embedding model never sees it. Prepend it yourself. A heading is also emitted as a chunk of its own, so skip the case where a chunk is its heading: 

for (const chunk of chunks) {
    const heading = chunk.metadata.closestHeading;
    const textToEmbed = heading && heading !== chunk.text
        ? `${heading}\n\n${chunk.text}`
        : chunk.text;

    // Embed textToEmbed. Store chunk.metadata next to the vector,
    // for filtering and for citations.
}

Sizes in Tokens, and Other Strategies

Sizes are counted in characters by default. To count tokens, pass a lengthFunction: your tokenizer's counter goes in, and maxChunkSize becomes a token budget.

Two more strategies are there when structure is not what you want. fixed-size is the familiar recursive splitter with overlap. semantic cuts where the topic shifts, using an embedding function that you supply.

Measure It on Your Own Documents

I am not going to quote a benchmark here. Retrieval numbers do not travel well between corpora, and the only result that matters is the one on your documents. What I can offer is the experiment worth running on your own files:

  1. Collect a few dozen real questions, and make sure some can only be answered from a table.
  2. For each question, note which passage of which document holds the answer.
  3. Index the documents twice: once with a fixed-size splitter, once with structural chunks.
  4. For each index, count how often the right passage shows up in the top results.

Pay attention to the table questions. That is where the two approaches differ most, and where a wrong answer is hardest to notice.

Summary

Stop treating documents as strings of characters. The structure an author put into a document is information, and a retrieval pipeline that flattens it first is working with less than it was given.

Cut at boundaries, keep tables whole or repeat their headers, and make sure every chunk knows where in the document it came from.
